context_title:
Your task is to take the provided technical description and rewrite it as a single, comprehensive prompt. Write it as if you were about to build the entire system from scratch: describe step by step, from beginning to end, exactly what you will construct and how you will construct it. The wording must be clear, explicit, and complete so that any language model can fully understand and follow the instructions without ambiguity. If the technical description refers to re‑implementing an existing software, do not include or mention the original software’s name in the prompt. Do not add any role‑playing, personalization, or polite filler phrases (e.g., ‘You are a software developer’, ‘As an expert’, ‘Please kindly’). The prompt must remain strictly technical, objective, and instruction‑focused. Absolutely no simplified, mock, placeholder, dummy, simulated, or fake content is allowed. You must require the full software with (all) file(s), in complete, unabridged, production‑ready code. Read it letter by letter, line by line, from beginning to end—you need to understand and remember every little detail! Always read and retain every single character of the provided text content in memory, ensuring no detail is overlooked. 
Build a complete, production-ready autonomous multi-agent orchestration platform from scratch. Deliver a real, runnable codebase with all required source files, dependency manifests, database migrations, infrastructure configuration, automated tests, API documentation, environment-variable template, container configuration, and operational documentation. Do not use mock implementations, placeholder endpoints, dummy data, simulated integrations, pseudocode, ellipses, TODO markers, incomplete functions, or omitted sections. Do not reproduce another product’s branding, proprietary prompts, private implementation details, or undocumented behavior. Use independently designed code and documented third-party interfaces only.

The platform must accept natural-language tasks, uploaded documents, structured data, URLs, images, and videos; determine whether a task should be answered directly or executed as a multi-step workflow; create a durable execution plan; invoke safe, schema-validated capabilities; execute code in isolated environments; validate intermediate and final results; preserve state across interruptions; expose real-time progress; and deliver verifiable artifacts to the user.

Implement the system as a modular service-oriented application. Use Python 3.12 for backend services, FastAPI for HTTP and WebSocket APIs, PostgreSQL for durable relational state, Redis for queues and short-lived coordination, an object store compatible with S3 for artifacts, and a container-or microVM-based isolated execution runtime. Use React, TypeScript, and a modern component-based frontend framework for the web interface. Use Docker Compose for local development and provide Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts for production deployment. Pin every dependency to a compatible version and include reproducible installation and deployment instructions.

Create the following backend modules and ensure that every module has clear interfaces, typed request and response schemas, structured logging, error handling, metrics, health checks, and unit and integration tests.

Create an intake service that receives user messages, file uploads, URLs, task configuration, and optional preferred output formats. Validate payload sizes, MIME types, authentication, authorization, rate limits, and tenant ownership. Normalize all accepted input into a durable task record containing a unique task identifier, user identifier, workspace identifier, input references, task status, timestamps, policy settings, budget settings, and initial execution context.

Create a task classification service that evaluates whether the request is suitable for direct response, information retrieval, document analysis, structured data processing, software generation, web interaction, code execution, multimodal analysis, or a composite workflow. The classifier must emit a validated structured result with task category, confidence score, risk level, required capabilities, estimated cost, estimated latency, and the selected execution tier. Use conservative routing for sensitive, irreversible, costly, or externally visible actions. Require explicit confirmation before actions that create accounts, spend money, send external messages, alter production infrastructure, expose private data, or perform any irreversible action.

Create a strategic planner that transforms a complex task into a directed acyclic graph of typed subtasks. Each subtask must contain an identifier, parent task identifier, objective, dependencies, inputs, expected outputs, acceptance criteria, required capability class, maximum retry count, maximum time budget, maximum cost budget, risk level, and execution status. The planner must identify independent subtasks that may run concurrently, serialize the resulting graph into PostgreSQL, and write a human-readable plan artifact to object storage. Generate multiple candidate plans when the task is complex, score them using estimated utility, tool reliability, cost, latency, risk, and expected confidence, then persist the selected plan together with its score and alternatives.

Implement a durable execution state machine with explicit states: CREATED, CLASSIFYING, PLANNING, AWAITING_APPROVAL, QUEUED, RUNNING, VALIDATING, REPAIRING, AGGREGATING, REVIEWING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, and BLOCKED. Enforce valid transitions transactionally. Record every transition as an immutable event with actor, timestamp, reason, correlation identifier, and relevant metadata. Support restart-safe recovery from the last completed checkpoint. Ensure that retries are idempotent and that repeated delivery or worker failure cannot corrupt task state.

Create an orchestrator that reads the task graph, schedules runnable subtasks, honors dependency completion, enforces tenant limits, applies per-task budgets, and caps concurrent isolated executions. Use a queue-based worker model. Implement configurable concurrency controls at global, tenant, task, and capability levels. For independent tasks, dispatch workers in parallel; for dependent tasks, wait until all required predecessor outputs are validated. Use cancellation tokens, timeouts, exponential backoff, circuit breakers, and bounded retry policies. Detect repeated failing action patterns and stop runaway loops before budgets are exceeded.

Implement specialized worker types for research, document extraction, browser automation, data analysis, code generation, code execution, artifact generation, multimodal analysis, verification, and synthesis. Every worker must receive only the minimal context required for its assigned subtask. Every worker must return a strict structured result containing status, output references, evidence references, tool-call records, validation notes, error details where applicable, elapsed time, resource usage, and confidence estimate. Prevent direct uncontrolled sharing of raw context between workers; use scoped artifacts, access-controlled storage paths, and typed result contracts.

Create a capability registry with stable capability definitions and JSON Schema or OpenAPI-compatible input and output specifications. Do not dynamically redefine capability schemas during a task. Implement a context-aware authorization layer that determines which capabilities are permitted for each state, task type, tenant policy, and risk level. Validate every capability request before execution. Apply allowlists for network destinations, filesystem paths, package sources, command classes, and integration scopes. Require elevated approval for sensitive capabilities.

Implement a web research capability using documented search and retrieval providers. Store source URL, retrieval timestamp, content hash, extracted text, publisher metadata, and retrieval confidence for every source. Do not treat search-result snippets as sufficient evidence when the original source can be retrieved. Support source deduplication by URL canonicalization, content hashing, semantic similarity, and entity normalization. Require cross-source verification for factual claims marked as high impact or low confidence. Preserve claim-to-source provenance so each final factual assertion can be audited.

Implement a browser automation capability in an isolated browser profile. Support navigation, reading rendered content, clicking, scrolling, form entry, file download, screenshot capture, and controlled JavaScript execution where policy permits. Keep a complete action log including URL, timestamp, action type, selector or coordinate reference, result, and screenshot or DOM snapshot references. Stop and request approval before submitting forms, making purchases, sending messages, logging into sensitive systems, or accepting legally binding terms.

Implement a secure code execution capability using ephemeral isolated runtimes. Use microVMs or hardened containers with non-root users, read-only base images, restricted Linux capabilities, per-execution network policy, CPU limits, memory limits, disk quotas, wall-clock timeouts, process limits, and separate writable workspaces. Attach only task-scoped input artifacts and a controlled output directory. Capture stdout, stderr, exit code, execution duration, resource metrics, generated files, and a machine-readable completion manifest. Enforce that execution output includes a validated result object with status, summary, generated artifact list, and diagnostics. Scan generated artifacts for secrets and unsafe content before promotion to shared storage.

Implement a code-generation workflow that converts a software-oriented subtask into an explicit technical specification, file tree, interfaces, database schema, dependency list, test plan, and acceptance criteria before implementation begins. Require approval before beginning a new deployable application when the user has requested a review gate. Generate complete source files, not partial fragments. Run formatting, static analysis, dependency checks, unit tests, integration tests, security scans, build steps, and smoke tests in the isolated runtime. If a test fails, create a bounded repair subtask that includes the failure evidence, affected files, reproduction command, and acceptance criterion. Re-run the relevant validation suite after each repair. Persist all generated source code and test reports as task artifacts.

Implement a data-analysis capability that loads supported structured formats, infers schemas, validates types, records transformations, generates reproducible analysis scripts, and creates requested deliverables such as CSV, XLSX, HTML reports, charts, or Markdown documents. For spreadsheets, define schemas before populating data, preserve formula provenance, validate formula ranges, verify totals and constraints, and test cross-sheet references. Do not silently invent missing values. Label derived values, assumptions, and confidence levels.

Implement a multimodal-analysis capability that accepts images and videos, extracts only observable attributes, records frame and timestamp references, preserves evidence links, and avoids unsupported claims about identity, intent, personality, health, or other latent traits. Process videos in bounded segments with frame sampling appropriate to duration and motion. Store structured visual observations, OCR results, object references, temporal events, and confidence values. Route sensitive biometric, medical, or identity-related tasks through policy restrictions and user confirmation where appropriate.

Create a validation engine that treats verification as a mandatory phase rather than a final text-only check. Implement schema validation for all worker outputs, executable probes for generated code, compilation and test execution, data integrity checks, source cross-checking, artifact existence checks, policy checks, and requirement coverage checks. Define confidence thresholds by task category. When validation fails, create a repair plan that targets the failed criterion, preserves the original evidence, and limits automatic repair attempts. Escalate to the user with clear evidence when the retry budget is exhausted, when external approval is required, or when uncertainty remains material.

Create a final aggregation service that receives only validated subtask outputs. Resolve duplicate results and conflicts using source quality, recency, directness, verifier confidence, and consistency with the task requirements. Produce final artifacts in requested formats. For factual reports, include inline citations or linked provenance entries that identify the source, excerpt location, retrieval time, and confidence. For generated files, include artifact metadata, checksums, sizes, content types, and download links. Preserve a final machine-readable manifest of requirements, completed subtasks, validation results, known limitations, and artifact inventory.

Create an independent review service that compares the original user requirements with the proposed final output. It must identify missing requirements, unsupported claims, incomplete artifacts, unmet acceptance criteria, policy violations, and unresolved validation failures. If review fails, transition the task to REPAIRING, add corrective subtasks to the task graph, and resume execution from the relevant checkpoint. Only mark a task COMPLETED when all mandatory requirements and validations have passed or when any unresolved limitation is explicitly presented to the user.

Implement persistent memory in separate layers. Store immutable event history for auditability. Store task-level working state in PostgreSQL and task-scoped artifacts in object storage. Store optional long-term workspace knowledge in a retrieval system with tenant isolation, explicit retention policies, provenance metadata, and deletion support. Do not rely on an LLM conversation window as the authoritative source of state. Generate compact, restorable state summaries for model context while retaining full raw logs and artifacts externally. Use append-only serialization for events and deterministic key ordering for structured context.

Implement model-provider adapters behind a provider-neutral interface. The interface must support chat generation, structured output, embeddings, vision input, streaming, tool or capability selection, token usage reporting, retries, and provider-specific error normalization. Load provider credentials only from environment variables or a managed secret store. Never expose credentials in logs, responses, artifacts, browser sessions, or generated source files. Support fallback routing only when policy permits and preserve the model, configuration, and reason for every routing decision in the audit trail.

Implement a security layer based on least privilege and zero-trust boundaries. Authenticate users and services using modern token-based authentication. Authorize every task, artifact, integration, and runtime action against workspace-scoped permissions. Encrypt data in transit and at rest. Store secrets in a dedicated secret manager. Redact personally identifiable information and secrets from logs by default. Maintain audit logs for authentication, authorization, policy decisions, capability requests, execution events, artifact access, and administrative actions. Add rate limiting, abuse detection, network egress controls, content-security protections, dependency vulnerability scanning, and secure defaults for all services.

Build a responsive web interface with authentication, workspace selection, task creation, file upload, URL submission, approval prompts, live task timeline, plan graph visualization, subtask states, worker logs, artifact browser, source provenance display, validation results, retry history, cancellation controls, budget indicators, and final-result rendering. Use WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for real-time updates. Do not expose secret values, raw hidden prompts, internal reasoning traces, or unredacted sensitive telemetry. Provide accessible semantic markup, keyboard navigation, proper error states, loading states, and mobile-responsive layouts.

Expose a documented REST API and streaming endpoint set. Include endpoints for task creation, task retrieval, task cancellation, approval decisions, artifact upload, artifact download, task event streams, workspace configuration, integration configuration, health checks, readiness checks, metrics, and administrative audit retrieval. Publish OpenAPI documentation generated from the application schemas. Enforce pagination, filtering, authorization, input validation, and consistent error response contracts.

Provide database migrations for all persistent entities, including users, workspaces, memberships, tasks, subtasks, dependency edges, events, approvals, artifacts, source records, claims, validation runs, execution attempts, budgets, policies, integrations, and audit logs. Add indexes for scheduler queries, task status queries, workspace isolation, event replay, artifact lookup, and provenance retrieval. Use transactions and optimistic locking or equivalent concurrency control for state transitions and scheduler updates.

Include automated tests covering authentication, authorization, input validation, state transitions, DAG scheduling, retry behavior, cancellation, budget enforcement, capability schema validation, browser-action approval gates, sandbox isolation assumptions, artifact access control, source provenance, validation failure handling, aggregation conflict resolution, WebSocket updates, database migrations, and end-to-end task execution. Include load tests for concurrent task scheduling and resilience tests for worker termination, queue redelivery, database restart, object-store failure, provider timeout, and partial execution recovery.

Provide local development and production operations files. Include Dockerfiles, Docker Compose configuration, environment-variable template, startup scripts, migration commands, test commands, lint commands, formatting commands, dependency lockfiles, CI pipeline configuration, Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts, ingress configuration, persistent volume configuration, secret references, autoscaling configuration, monitoring dashboards, alert rules, and backup and restore instructions. Ensure all services have readiness and liveness endpoints and graceful shutdown behavior.

Use explicit acceptance criteria for every core workflow. A direct-answer task must produce a response without unnecessary execution. A research task must store and expose source provenance. A code task must produce complete files and passing validation evidence. A data task must preserve transformations and validation results. A long-running task must survive process restart and resume from a durable checkpoint. A cancelled task must stop scheduling new work and clean up ephemeral runtimes. A failed task must preserve diagnostics and artifacts. A sensitive external action must not occur without approval. A completed task must have a final review record and an artifact manifest.

Output the complete repository as a file-by-file implementation. Include every source file in full, all configuration files, all migration files, all test files, all documentation files, and all deployment files. Do not omit implementation details. Do not provide explanatory filler outside the repository content.
